• Common name: Water milfoil
  • Scientific name: Myriophyllum elatinoides (Myriophyllum quitense)
  • Difficulty: easy to medium
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Optimal pH: 6.0 – 8.0
  • Optimal GH: 2 – 12
  • Optimal temperature: 20 – 26°C (68 – 79°F)
  • Substrate: any (can float)
  • Can be grown emersed: no
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Placement: midground or background
  • Aquarium size: 60 – 100 cm high (12 to 40 inches)
  • CO2: not required
  • Propagation: cuttings
  • Colour: green
Myriophyllum elatinoides can be found in South America (Chile, southern Argentina), Mexico, the Falkland Islands, Tasmania, New Zealand, Australia, and China.
This species generally occurs in irrigation systems and channel sites with high light availability and low water turbidity.
Due to its significant size and very fast growth rate, Water Milfoil is only suited to larger (especially taller) aquariums starting from 80 litres (20 gallons).

Planting: Myriophyllum elatinoides has long stems and is generally planted along the sides of an aquarium, in the midground or background. Do not plant the stems too close to each other (keep them at least 5 cm / 2 inches apart); in cramped conditions the plant often drops its leaves. Use tweezers to gently place the stems into the substrate to avoid damage. It can also be used as a floating plant or tied to driftwood. If left floating, it will find a place it likes and eventually root.

Propagation: By cuttings. Cut the upper portion of the stem with sharp scissors just above a leaf node; the ideal cutting is about 10 cm (4 inches) long. Make a hole in the substrate about 3 – 4 cm deep, place the stems gently in the hole and cover with substrate. In time, healthy stems develop roots and grow into new plants.

Problems:

  • Loss of leaves: a sign of insufficient light. If the plant is grown too thick, the lower part lacks light and sheds leaves. Solution: thin out or trim the plant when it becomes dense so light reaches all parts.
  • Fragile: the stem seems thick and hardy but is actually soft and easily broken. Solution: be careful during maintenance.
  • Overgrowth: under high light, nutrients and CO2, it can grow like a weed and fill the tank within weeks. Solution: trim stems regularly.
  • Discoloration: may be triggered by nutrient deficiency (nitrogen (NO3) and phosphates (PO4)). Solution: use liquid fertilizers periodically and test the water to ensure ample nutrients.

Quarantine: Unless the plant is certainly safe (for example grown in vitro in an undamaged, unopened pot), quarantine and disinfect it first. Do not introduce a new plant to the tank right after buying it: it can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly, damselfly nymphs, etc.), and may contain pesticide residues that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Temperature: Although Myriophyllum elatinoides can grow even in cold water (down to 10°C / 50°F), the optimal temperature ranges from 20 – 26°C (68 – 80°F).

pH: 6.0 – 8.0.

Hardness: It can grow in soft and hard water, GH 2 – 12. However, it was also noticed that in soft water it grows slower.

Lighting: Water Milfoil requires at least medium-high lighting (30–50 PAR). Maintain a standard photoperiod of 10-12 hours daily. It does not tolerate long-term shading well. With insufficient lighting, the stem elongates, becomes leggy, and density decreases.

Flow: It tolerates moderate water movement, but avoid strong currents.

Substrate: This plant mostly obtains nutrients from the water column. It does not require a nutrient-rich substrate since its root system is not well-developed.

CO2: Although CO2 addition promotes growth significantly, a pressurized CO2 system is not mandatory; it is optional.

Fertilization: It needs moderate to high nutrient levels (especially phosphorus and nitrogen). Experiments showed that although phosphorus can be taken up through the leaves and roots, leaf uptake appears to be the preferential mechanism. Therefore, regular dosing of liquid plant fertilizers (2-3 times a week) is required.

If you keep shrimp in the tank, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Etymology: "Myriophyllum" derives from the Greek "myrio" (numerous, many) and "phyllum" (leaf). "Elatinoides" suggests a resemblance to plants in the genus Elatine.

Taxonomy: Distinguishing some Myriophyllum species is difficult due to their striking resemblance; one study suggests considering M. elatinoides a synonym of M. quitense. Family: Haloragaceae; order: Haloragales.

Description: A perennial submersed or floating plant with bushy green foliage, typically 60 – 100 cm tall and about 5 – 7 cm wide. The stem is soft but relatively thick (2 – 4 mm). Leaves are usually whorled, sometimes opposite or alternate; submerged leaves are 3- or 4-pinnate. Colour ranges from pale green to emerald. The inflorescence typically forms a terminal spike with small, four-parted flowers. The root system is weak.

Benefits:

  • Aquascape: suits jungle or Dutch style aquascapes.
  • Hiding place: cover and shade for invertebrates and small fish.
  • Foraging: provides biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Reduces nitrates: as a fast grower it takes up phosphorus and nitrogen, and has been reported to remove nutrients, heavy metals and organic contaminants.
  • Reduces algae: it outcompetes algae and cyanobacteria for nutrients.

Its biomass has been reported to be usable as a high-protein feed for livestock and poultry.

Conclusion: A beautiful, easy stem plant needing medium to strong light, growing in any substrate (even floating) without CO2. However, without control it can overshadow everything in the tank.
